title: November minutes expose the disputed capacity estimate behind a 6–3 rise to 4.85%
summary: At its 2–3 November meeting the Board voted 6–3 to raise the cash rate from 4.60% to 4.85%. The minutes were released on 17 November. Three members preferred to wait after 100 basis points of tightening earlier in the year, including the September increase. The six supporting a further move thought the forecast inflation overshoot and risk of rising expectations outweighed the risk of inducing excessive slack. Their concern extended beyond oil. Staff had revised up its estimate of the unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation, so the observed rise in unemployment no longer produced the disinflationary signal that earlier forecasts would have assigned it (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

Both headline and underlying inflation exceeded the August forecast in the September quarter. Fuel made the largest contribution to the headline surprise. The more informative domestic reading was higher inflation in market services excluding telecommunications and domestic travel, a group generally responsive to domestic resource pressure. Staff projected headline and underlying inflation staying above 3% until late 2027, then returning to the 2.5% target midpoint around mid-2028. This was a later return than in August despite a higher interest-rate path. The October annual headline figure was likely to jump as the previous year’s household subsidies dropped out of the comparison. Such arithmetic can change a conspicuous CPI reading without showing that current month’s domestic demand had accelerated (Economic conditions).

Crude and refined petroleum prices had risen 20–25% since August. The market curves used in the forecast implied a decline in oil of roughly US$30 a barrel over two years. For those curves to be realised, some resolution of the disruption would be needed. Staff also assumed that firms would pass roughly two-thirds of the added conflict-related costs on. Domestic capacity pressure accounted for a large part of the projected high underlying inflation over the coming year. Indirect pressure from conflict-related costs was expected to become a noticeable contributor by early 2027. These are two separate judgements. A different oil path changes the size of the initial cost, while demand conditions influence what fraction reaches retail customers (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

Staff revised the estimated unemployment rate consistent with low and stable inflation, often called the NAIRU, upwards. Repeated inflation surprises, labour and other input costs, sectoral competition for staff and survey evidence of above-average capacity use supported the change. Yet the Wage Price Index had evolved broadly as projected, and wage growth on individually negotiated arrangements, normally sensitive to labour conditions, had slowed. Weak productivity could reconcile moderate wage growth with high costs per unit of output. Alternatively, factors besides an underestimated NAIRU might explain the inflation surprise. Monthly market-services inflation had slowed within the quarter. The series was too short for seasonal adjustment, limiting what members could conclude from that decline (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

Unemployment had risen half a percentage point over six months. Staff associated much of the surprise with increased labour supply and participation, while employment growth remained close to expectations. The revised projection had unemployment reaching 5.1% by end-2028, around a quarter point higher than previously projected, with much less change in the outlook for employment growth. Demand and productive capacity were projected to return to balance around mid-2027 before spare capacity opened. If the rise in unemployment instead signalled a sharper fall in job finding or demand, the employment cost of further restraint would be higher. That distinction formed part of the minority’s case for waiting (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

Funding conditions varied sharply by borrower. Housing activity and new lending had weakened, particularly investor loans affected by tax changes. Scheduled payments relative to income were near their 2024 peak, yet large offsets, low arrears and a stable share of borrowers steadily running down balances indicated a degree of resilience. A decline in additional repayments could help households maintain spending. Business borrowing meanwhile remained strong. Data-centre developers raised debt equivalent to at least a fifth of the increase in business debt during the year. Investors had become more discerning about prospective returns and debt-service capacity at some AI firms. Some Australian operators experienced falling equity prices and wider spreads. Tighter funding for private credit lenders also threatened financing for residential development. Strong aggregate credit did not guarantee continued funding for the marginal project (Financial conditions).

Both the existing cash rate and the market path were above the top of the central neutral-rate estimates considered. Lower global saving associated with fiscal deficits and stronger investment, including in AI, may nonetheless have raised equilibrium rates, reducing the restraint of any given nominal setting. Longer government yields remained above early-August levels, with longer-term inflation compensation broadly stable. A higher term premium would add relatively limited household restraint given the short-term basis of much Australian borrowing. The nominal trade-weighted currency was about 5% higher than at the start of the year. Immediately before the decision, overnight-indexed swaps implied roughly an 85% probability of a rise and about 35 basis points of cumulative tightening from the then-current rate by mid-2027. These price observations help establish the pre-decision benchmark, not the response to the minutes two weeks later (Financial conditions).

The majority judged that delaying action risked households and firms raising medium-term expectations after a prolonged spell above target. Some survey evidence supported that concern, but the Business Outlook Scenarios Survey had a short history and established market measures remained relatively well anchored. The minority gave more weight to incomplete transmission from earlier hikes and the possibility that falling housing turnover would depress both transaction activity and purchases associated with moving house. A reassessment of data-centre investment returns could amplify weakness. They accepted that further tightening might prove necessary. They disputed the case for doing so before more evidence arrived. The debate therefore turns on whether persistence and deteriorating demand can be distinguished quickly enough from observations of different vintage and quality, rather than on a mechanical threshold in the unemployment or headline CPI rate (Considerations for monetary policy and The decision).

questions.question: Would a higher estimate of sustainable unemployment improve real-time forecasts independently of the inflation surprise used to infer it?
questions.detail: Compare original-vintage projections with and without the revised NAIRU, using subsequent labour-market behaviour, market-services inflation, unit labour costs and individual wage arrangements. Include alternative productivity paths and separate participation from firm hiring. A revision that fits past inflation mechanically but fails to explain new recruitment, wage or price outcomes would offer weak support for increasing restraint.

questions.question: What fraction of the energy shock reached customers, and on whose balance sheet did the remainder sit?
questions.detail: Match fuel and refined-product input costs to subsequent selling prices, gross margins and volumes, distinguishing direct fuel from downstream products. Compare firms with different energy hedges and demand exposure. Set the estimated pass-through and its uncertainty against the staff’s two-thirds assumption. A low early estimate might reflect delays in procurement rather than lasting absorption by shareholders or workers.

questions.question: Could the housing and AI investment slowdowns reinforce one another through financing?
questions.detail: Track mortgage approvals, transactions and moving-related purchases alongside developer credit, private credit funding, data-centre issuance and project delays. Distinguish amounts raised from capital actually spent, including imported equipment. Identify common lenders and maturity dates where observable. The minority’s adverse case becomes more plausible if funding changes predict a joint contraction in activity beyond the usual historical effect of weaker housing turnover.
